did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word 'zonah' appears here and is often translated 'prostitute', but scholars note it can sometimes describe a woman who ran a household or hosted travelers.
The spies were sent from Shittim — the Israelites' last camp before crossing the Jordan, in the plains of Moab east of the river.
Houses then often had flat roofs used for sleeping and drying flax, so hiding people on the roof was practical.
City gates were both defensive and administrative hubs; closing the gate signaled a lockdown and protection from attackers.
The term 'Yam Suph' appears here — in Biblical Hebrew it can literally mean 'Sea of Reeds', so translating it as the 'Red Sea' is not always straightforward.
Some houses were built into the city wall, and a window in the outer wall made it possible to lower someone outside by rope.
The word 'chesed' here carries the idea of loyalty and covenant obligation — more than a one-time act of kindness.
The scarlet cord left in the window acted as a clear sign for the troops to recognize the house to be spared; a bright red marker is easy to spot.
